edges.description: Loss of SCEH blocks the valine catabolic pathway at the hydration of methacrylyl-CoA and acryloyl-CoA, causing these reactive intermediates to accumulate.
edges.target: Impaired valine catabolism and reactive-metabolite accumulation

edges.description: Despite SCEH being a beta-oxidation-spiral enzyme, mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation flux is largely preserved because of overlapping hydratase activities.
The accumulated reactive thioesters covalently react with sulfhydryl groups (cysteine, glutathione, cysteamine) and damage mitochondrial proteins, including the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.
intermediate_mechanisms: Reactive methacrylyl-CoA/acryloyl-CoA adduct formation on sulfhydryl-bearing mitochondrial proteins
edges.source: Impaired valine catabolism and reactive-metabolite accumulation
edges.target: Reactive-metabolite mitochondrial and pyruvate dehydrogenase toxicity

edges.description: Secondary PDH and respiratory-chain dysfunction, together with direct metabolite toxicity, produce bilateral symmetric basal ganglia (putaminal) necrotizing lesions characteristic of Leigh / Leigh-like disease.
intermediate_mechanisms: Secondary pyruvate dehydrogenase and respiratory-chain deficiency causing neuronal energy failure
edges.source: Reactive-metabolite mitochondrial and pyruvate dehydrogenase toxicity

edges.description: Basal ganglia degeneration produces dystonia, a hallmark motor feature.
Progressive basal ganglia and white-matter injury manifests as developmental delay and regression.
intermediate_mechanisms: Progressive neuronal loss in basal ganglia and associated structures

edges.description: Elevated lactate reports the secondary bioenergetic (PDH and respiratory-chain) dysfunction downstream of the enzyme defect.
edges.source: Reactive-metabolite mitochondrial and pyruvate dehydrogenase toxicity

evidence.snippet: The patient presented with hypotonia, metabolic acidosis, and developmental delay.

nodes.description: Dystonia arising from basal ganglia degeneration; a hallmark movement disorder and a target of dietary therapy.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical improvements after treatment with a low-valine and low-fat diet in a pediatric patient with enoyl-CoA hydratase, short chain 1 (ECHS1) deficiency.
evidence.snippet: He presented severe dystonia, hyperlordosis, moderate to severe kyphoscoliosis, great difficulty in walking, and severe dysarthria.

nodes.description: Biallelic pathogenic variants in ECHS1 markedly reduce short-chain enoyl-CoA hydratase (SCEH/crotonase) protein and enzyme activity in the mitochondrial matrix. SCEH is a multifunctional hydratase acting on substrates from several pathways, catalyzing the second step of the fatty-acid beta-oxidation spiral and an early hydration step of valine catabolism.

evidence.reference_title: ECHS1 mutations cause combined respiratory chain deficiency resulting in Leigh syndrome.
evidence.snippet: The human ECHS1 gene encodes the short-chain enoyl coenzyme A hydratase, the enzyme that catalyzes the second step of β-oxidation of fatty acids in the mitochondrial matrix.

evidence.reference_title: ECHS1 mutations cause combined respiratory chain deficiency resulting in Leigh syndrome.
evidence.snippet: ECHS1 protein expression was severely depleted in the patient's skeletal muscle and patient-derived myoblasts; a marked decrease in enzyme activity was also evident in patient-derived myoblasts.

evidence.reference_title: ECHS1 mutations in Leigh disease: a new inborn error of metabolism affecting valine metabolism.
evidence.snippet: ECHS1 activity was markedly decreased in cultured fibroblasts from both siblings, ECHS1 protein was undetectable by immunoblot analysis and transfection of patient cells with wild-type ECHS1 rescued ECHS1 activity.

evidence.reference_title: ECHS1 mutations in Leigh disease: a new inborn error of metabolism affecting valine metabolism.
evidence.snippet: Both children were compound heterozygous for a c.473C > A (p.A158D) missense mutation and a c.414+3G>C splicing mutation in ECHS1.

nodes.description: SCEH deficiency blocks valine catabolism at the hydration of the reactive thioesters methacrylyl-CoA and acryloyl-CoA. These highly reactive intermediates accumulate and are considered the principal drivers of neurotoxicity, in parallel with the biochemically and clinically similar HIBCH deficiency of the adjacent valine-pathway step.
nodes.id: Impaired valine catabolism and reactive-metabolite accumulation

evidence.reference_title: ECHS1 mutations in Leigh disease: a new inborn error of metabolism affecting valine metabolism.
evidence.snippet: The highly reactive metabolites methacrylyl-CoA and acryloyl-CoA accumulate in deficiencies of both ECHS1 and HIBCH and are probably responsible for the brain pathology in both disorders.

nodes.description: The convergent bioenergetic and toxic insult manifests as bilateral symmetric basal ganglia (especially putaminal) degeneration with necrotizing/cavitating lesions, the neuropathological substrate of the Leigh-syndrome phenotype and its motor and developmental sequelae.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical and biochemical characterization of four patients with mutations in ECHS1.
evidence.snippet: All patients presented with lactic acidosis. The first two patients presented with vacuolating leukoencephalopathy and basal ganglia abnormalities.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical improvements after treatment with a low-valine and low-fat diet in a pediatric patient with enoyl-CoA hydratase, short chain 1 (ECHS1) deficiency.
evidence.snippet: The Leigh syndrome phenotype is the most frequently reported form of the disease.

nodes.description: Reactive valine-pathway intermediates deplete cellular thiol pools and damage mitochondrial proteins, producing a secondary pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) deficiency and secondary respiratory-chain dysfunction. This bioenergetic failure links the primary enzyme defect to the Leigh-like neurodegeneration, mirroring other mitochondrial energy-metabolism disorders.
nodes.id: Reactive-metabolite mitochondrial and pyruvate dehydrogenase toxicity

evidence.reference_title: Clinical and biochemical characterization of four patients with mutations in ECHS1.
evidence.snippet: In severely affected patients SCEH deficiency can cause a secondary pyruvate dehydrogenase deficiency contributing to the clinical presentation.

evidence.reference_title: Clinical and biochemical characterization of four patients with mutations in ECHS1.
